newsitem.title: USA: U.S. refuses to rule out new Iraq strikes.
newsitem.headline: U.S. refuses to rule out new Iraq strikes.

text.p: The CIA said on Thursday Iraqi troops were leaving northern Iraq, but the State Department said they remained a threat and refused to rule out new U.S. attacks on President Saddam Hussein's forces.

As U.S. warplanes kept watch on an expanded no-fly zone in southern Iraq for the second day, U.S. Central Intelligence Agency Director John Deutch appeared to contradict news reports that Iraqi troops and tanks were again attacking Kurds near Arbil in northern Iraq.

"We are seeing the withdrawal of the mechanized and armoured units from the Kurdish territories in northern Iraq back to their garrisons fairly systematically," Deutch said in testimony before the Senate Intelligence Committee.

But State Department spokesman Glyn Davies cautioned against taking a narrow view of Iraqi deployments, saying that Saddam had introduced a "massive security presence" in the Kurdish area under cover of troop deployments.

"So his troops remain very much a threat to Iraq's civilian population in the north. And we will continue to assess that threat, and indeed the threat elsewhere in Iraq, as we decide on U.S. actions," Davies said.

In Paris, U.S. State Department officials also denied that Secretary of State Warren Christopher had assured Frech President Jacques Chirac and Foreign Minister Herve de Charette during a visit on Thursday that the U.S. "Desert Strike" cruise missile attacks on Iraq were finished.
"We retain the option and the right to use force if necessary," spokesman Nicholas Burns told reporters.
A massive Iraqi attack on Arbil last weekend triggered U.S. cruise missile strikes against Saddam's air defences in southern Iraq on Tuesday and Wednesday.
In addition, the United States expanded a no-fly zone to cover most of southern Iraq as part.
The Pentagon also challenged the reports that Iraqi troops and tanks were again attacking Kurds near Arbil.
"We don't see it happening. We don't see any attacks or massing of tanks in the area between Arbil and Sulaimaniya," said Navy Lieutenant Commander Scott Campbell.

Saddam has vowed to ignore the exclusion zones in both northern and southern Iraq, where they have been enforced by allied warplanes since the aftermath of the 1991 Gulf War that ousted his invasion forces from Kuwait.

Although President Bill Clinton proclaimed on Wednesday that the cruise missile strikes had taught Saddam a necessary lesson, two senior members of Congress said on Thursday Clinton might have to resume such attacks to drive the lesson home.
"Saddam has not been discouraged by our attacks," Republican Senator Richard Lugar of Indiana said in an interview on Fox television.
"We are going to have to do more to get the word across to him ... make certain that he is badly crippled, that his military instruments are crippled."
Democratic Representative Lee Hamilton of Indiana concurred with that view in the same interview. "I certainly think additional power may be necessary here against Saddam Hussein," he said.
Lugar and Hamilton are two of the more influential foreign policy voices in their respective houses of Congress.

United Nations guards and foreign aid workers in northern Iraq said on Thursday that rival Kurdish factions had clashed near a strategic bridge at the village of Degala as Iraqi government troops and armour stood by and did not intervene.
Their reports from the field, monitored in Arbil, said fighting was heavy between forces of the Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP) and the Patriotic Union of Kurdistan (PUK).

But the PUK office in London said in a statement that 120 to 150 Iraqi tanks were in the area, heading in the direction of Koi Sanjaq. Heavy artillery and KDP fighters accompanied the tanks, the statement said.
Last weekend Baghdad's forces helped the KDP eject PUK fighters from Arbil, triggering the U.S. retaliation.
Sulaimaniya, a PUK stronghold, is 80 miles south of Arbil. Chamchamal is some 40 miles north of Sulaimaniya.
U.S. defence officials said the southern no-fly zone, established after the war to protect Shiite Moslems from Saddam's forces, was quiet early on Thursday.
